opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a big ambition, and I think it's worth unpacking why we even dare to say it out loud. When you look at how drug discovery has worked historically, it's been incredibly empirical. You have a disease hypothesis, you identify a target, and then you go through this long, expensive process of screening, synthesizing molecules, testing them in the lab, and iterating. Most of that iteration is trial and error, and most programs fail. It takes a decade or more and billions of dollars to get a single drug to patients.

What we believe at Isomorphic is that a huge amount of that process can move from the wet lab into the computer. If you can build models that truly understand biology and chemistry at a molecular level — how proteins fold, how they interact with each other, how a small molecule binds to a pocket, what it does to the dynamics of the system — then you can explore that design space in silico, much faster and much more broadly than you ever could physically. AlphaFold was an early proof point that this kind of thing is possible, and with AlphaFold 3 we started to see models that understand not just protein structure but the interactions between proteins, nucleic acids, ligands — the actual stuff of drug design.

So the way I think about "solving all disease" is really about building a general drug design engine. Not a model for one target or one disease area, but a set of foundational models and a platform that can be pointed at any target, any modality, and rapidly generate high-quality drug candidates. If you get that generality right, then the same system that works on an oncology target should transfer to immunology, to neurodegeneration, to rare diseases that nobody's ever had the economic incentive to work on. That's where the "all" comes from — it's about removing the bottlenecks that make each new program a bespoke, decade-long effort.

Of course, we're not naive about it. Biology is enormously complex, and there are parts of the pipeline — clinical trials, understanding disease biology at the systems level — that AI won't collapse overnight. But we're working on real internal programs and with partners, and that grounding matters a lot. Every time we push a model against a real drug design problem, we learn where it breaks, and that feeds back into the research. That tight loop between frontier ML research and actual drug discovery is, I think, what's going to get us there.

r001.rationale: The response describes modeling molecular biology and designing drugs for targets, but does not say AI can reveal new biological pathways for therapeutic intervention.

r002.rationale: It identifies a general drug design engine and platform usable for any target or modality, with the same system transferring across disease areas.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So when we say "solve all diseases," I want to be precise about what we mean, because it sounds grandiose, and in a sense it is. But the way I think about it is less about a single breakthrough and more about changing the fundamental economics and timescales of drug discovery.

Right now, if you look at how a drug gets made, it takes something like ten to fifteen years and costs billions of dollars, and the vast majority of programs fail. And a huge part of that failure comes from the fact that we're operating with a very incomplete understanding of the biology. We make a hypothesis about a target, we try to design a molecule that interacts with it, and then we find out five years later in the clinic that something didn't work the way we thought it would.

What AlphaFold showed us, and what Isomorphic was really founded on, is that machine learning can give you a genuinely predictive model of a slice of biology. Structure prediction was the first slice. If you can predict how a protein folds, and then how it interacts with other proteins, with small molecules, with nucleic acids, you start to have a computational model of the molecular machinery of the cell. And once you have that, drug design becomes much more like engineering and much less like searching in the dark.

So the way I envision it is a kind of flywheel. You build models that are good enough to be useful on real drug programs. Those programs generate data, both from the models' own predictions and from the wet lab experiments that validate them. That data feeds back into better models. And each turn of that loop expands the set of targets you can go after. Things that were considered undruggable, because they didn't have a nice pocket or because they were too dynamic, become tractable.

The ambition to solve all diseases is really the ambition to make that loop general enough that you're not building a bespoke pipeline per disease. You're building a platform where the question for a new indication becomes, what's the biology, and can we design a molecule for it, rather than, do we have the ten-year budget to even try.

I'd also say we're not naive about this. Biology is the hardest domain there is for machine learning. The data is noisy, it's expensive to generate, and the models have to be right in ways that matter for patients. So we're deliberately combining a strong research culture, which comes from DeepMind, with real drug discovery experience, and running actual programs with partners so the models are tested against reality, not just benchmarks. That's the difference between an interesting paper and a medicine.

r001.rationale: The response describes modeling molecular biology and making previously difficult targets tractable, but does not say that AI understanding reveals new biological pathways for therapeutic intervention.

r002.rationale: It describes making the drug-discovery loop general enough to avoid a bespoke pipeline for each disease, using a platform to assess biology and design molecules across indications.

astra-6.text:
I think the way to understand that ambition is that we’re trying to build a general approach to drug discovery. If you can use AI to understand how a molecule will interact with a biological system, and then design a molecule that changes that system in the way you want, you have something that could apply across many different diseases.

Of course, solving a molecular design problem isn’t the same as curing a disease. You still need to understand what drives the disease, run experiments, and demonstrate that a treatment is safe and effective in patients. The opportunity is to make that whole process much more predictive—to learn from experiments and use that learning to design better ones.

So I see this as a progression: develop the underlying capabilities, prove they can produce useful medicines, and build toward increasingly general systems. ‘All diseases’ is an enormous ambition. The exciting idea is that improvements in the underlying technology could benefit many discovery programmes at once, rather than having to start from scratch for every disease.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using AI to predict molecule–biology interactions, but does not say that understanding disease biology reveals new pathways for therapeutic intervention.

r002.rationale: It describes a general AI approach to drug discovery that could apply across many diseases, with improvements benefiting multiple discovery programmes.

sol-6.1.text:
The way I think about it is that solving all disease is a direction of travel. It’s an incredibly ambitious mission, and getting there means fundamentally changing how we discover and design medicines.

At Isomorphic Labs, we’re trying to build AI models that can understand and predict biology well enough to help us do that. AlphaFold gives you a sense of what’s possible: something that looked extraordinarily difficult can become a problem where computational predictions are genuinely useful. The question is how far we can extend that capability—from understanding structures and interactions to designing molecules that produce the effect we want.

And that has to be a loop with experiments. You make a prediction, design a molecule, test it, and learn from what actually happens. Over time, you want that loop to become much more accurate and efficient, so that you can tackle a new disease without starting the whole discovery process from scratch.

There’s a huge amount of work between that vision and a medicine that helps a patient. But the exciting possibility is that we can build a general approach that improves across many different diseases, rather than making progress on each one in isolation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using AI to understand and predict biology and design molecules, but does not say this reveals new biological pathways for therapeutic intervention.

r002.rationale: It describes building a general approach that improves across many diseases and lets the team tackle new diseases without starting the discovery process from scratch.
